items.title: COVID exposed how thin most supply chains were
items.claim: During 2020-22, automotive production was held back by shortages of one component category in particular. Which was it?

options.text: Semiconductors (chips) — the global shortage cost the automotive industry an estimated $210 billion in lost revenue in 2021 alone (AlixPartners)

items.reveal:
When auto demand fell in spring 2020, car makers cancelled chip orders. Foundries (TSMC, Samsung) reallocated capacity to consumer electronics, where demand was surging. When car demand returned, chip capacity was booked out. Ford alone lost around 1.25 million units of production in 2021.

The US CHIPS Act (2022) and EU Chips Act (2023) responded with $50bn+ in subsidies for domestic semiconductor manufacturing — a direct strategic response to the disruption.
items.why: Multi-tier supply chains hide concentration risk. A car maker can have hundreds of direct suppliers but still depend on two or three foundries for chips.

items.title: The Hawthorne effect is real but smaller than the textbook story
items.claim: Elton Mayo's Hawthorne studies (1927-32) are taught as showing that worker productivity rose because of attention paid to them. What does re-analysis of the original data show?

options.text: The effect was even larger than originally reported

Levitt and List's 2011 re-analysis of original records suggests the 'Hawthorne effect' was much weaker than reported; productivity gains were largely explained by which workers were replaced and the Monday rebound after weekends
No data from the studies survived
The lighting reduction was actually the cause

items.reveal:
Steven Levitt and John List (American Economic Journal, 2011) accessed original Hawthorne Works data digitised by the University of Wisconsin. They found the famous 'productivity rose whatever you changed' pattern was much weaker than Mayo claimed and largely artifactual.

The broader 'human relations' school it spawned remained influential — but the founding evidence base was weaker than generations of textbooks suggested.
items.why: Iconic findings get retold long after the evidence has been challenged. Modern HR theory survives, but its founding study should be taught with caveats.

items.title: Ansoff said diversification was the riskiest growth strategy
items.claim: Igor Ansoff's 1957 'Strategies for Diversification' in Harvard Business Review introduced a 2x2 matrix. Which growth strategy did he flag as carrying highest risk?

options.text: Diversification (new product, new market) — combining product and market uncertainty multiplies risk

items.reveal:
Ansoff's matrix sequences risk: market penetration (existing product, existing market) is safest; product development and market development each add one source of uncertainty; diversification adds two.

Empirical work (Markides 1995, McKinsey 2010s) has supported this in aggregate: unrelated diversification destroys shareholder value more often than not. The 1960s conglomerate boom (ITT, Hanson) and its 1990s breakup vindicated Ansoff's warning.
items.why: Growth strategies look attractive on the upside; Ansoff's matrix forces you to articulate the downside risks for each route.
